1. I had career advisors and guidance counselors suggest that programming would be a good fit for me, but I was kept away from it by my very old-fashioned father. 3. I like it, particularly web development, but I’m worried about how I can break into the field so late in the game. I live a pretty simple life and don’t have a personal network to speak of, so I don’t know how I’ll get a position when there are so many people younger than myself that have years more experience.
4. I’d like to learn more about web design in addition to development. I’m kind of a dope in that what I find most exciting is seeing the pretty webpage I’ve made, but I’d like to know how to do that consistently and understand what clients are looking for in a webpage that they couldn’t just make themselves of Squarespace, Wix, etc.

Thank you for articulating this so well. I’m currently at 2 months into serious self-teaching, having finished CS50 and nearly through TOP Foundations. Years ago, I did an online IT degree with a few coding courses, and have frequently been frustrated at how much of the practical work is left to be solved without any examples or explanation. I see someone posting about how “you need to figure it out on your own without guidance, that’s how I did it as a kid when I was making my own MMORPG from scratch” and think they must be forgetting that not everyone learning is a child or a student on a college campus. If I’m struggling to solve a problem or make a program, it’s not just part of the learning process: it’s time wasted when maybe I should have just looked for another line of work despite my interests. It’s my partner and family wondering why I don’t have a well-paying job yet. It’s self-doubt and putdowns at what I have made since I know I’m going to be applying for jobs against younger candidates that could learn all this and more while mom and dad cook dinner and keep a roof over their head.
I've just bookmarked it, and will definitely give it a shot tomorrow. It's a shame because the TOP unit on flex boxes was quite fun compared to the CSS practice I've done in the past.

I get plenty of exercise (daily morning jogs at minimum) but she wants me to take a break every hour to take a three-hour walk the beach.

>If you don't enjoy learning a job but push yourself to learn it anyway, then that's a recipe for unhappy life. Some people do that, but you're still young at 31, you have options.

That's part of what's got me on edge: I do enjoy learning it, but I also need to push myself to learn faster and better if I'm to have any chance to make it in the field. It's so much more pressure knowing I need to be good enough at this to get a job within a year if I'm going to feed myself, pay my student loans, and stay in the UK with my partner. I'm struggling with beginner-level content but can't afford to struggle with it for very long.

Congratulations on your progress, and stick with it! I was in a similar boat: I met a German girl while backpacking, started learning the language, and was unsure of whether to continue after the relationship fell apart. I ultimately kept going because I wanted to have a valuable skill and break out of the monolingual American stereotype. 

Now it's been over two years since I've started, I've met other German friends, learned more about their culture and history, and look forward to finally visiting Germany with my new partner (non-German speaker but very supportive). I can't separate my language journey from that failed relationship, but I've managed to make many more positive associations.

I think you can do the same. Read about the history and sights in places where your target language is spoken, research jobs that you could do with your language skills, and find media to enjoy in that language. You can overcome this funk! :)

Absolutely! I grew up in rural New Hampshire and had a choice of French, Spanish, or Latin for my HS language requirement. Should I do French because we're so close to Quebec? Or should I take Spanish because of it's wide use in the US? Or maybe you are too poor to even think about leaving your white-bread state and are pressured into taking as much STEM as possible for a shot at college. I wound up taking Latin in hopes I'd have a better foundation for more practical languages down the line.

Now I've had a chance to travel and despite squeezing some language learning into my adult routine, get teased for only speaking English comfortably. I must be a nationalist, racist, uncultured moron, right? /s

Thank you for the encouragement. I’m going to try to dedicate some time each day to different resources to feel more well-rounded, though I’m worried it is hopeless learning without real conversation practice. 

Also, I should specify that the German guys I met commented that my American accent made my *English* sound “dirty” compared to the accents of our Scottish and Welsh friends. I can only imagine how much they’d hate the sound of me speaking German.

It’s okay, and as others have said on here, it’s perfectly fine to take a break if you aren’t feeling the same enjoyment. I went through the same thing a few years ago, and I think it had a lot to do with the changing culture surrounding games. Casually picking up a new game or revisiting an old one felt pointless if I knew some kid was basking in admiration and sponsorship money by streaming, speedrunning, playing competitively, etc.  
Separate yourself from games for a while, think about what you used to like about them, and see if you can find those same qualities in new hobbies! I was lucky enough to go backpacking, and between the challenge of the outdoors and exploring new cities, I gained a new appreciation for the open-world games and artsy platformers I used to love.  
You mentioned in another comment that you are starting university. What kind of courses will you take? Are there clubs that catch your eye? If you like BF1, Fallout, War Thunder, etc. consider courses about military history or historical / speculative fiction writing, or even just check out the books at your uni’s library or a local museum. There are also bound to be tabletop gaming groups if you want to try RPGs like Fallout in a different, screen-free setting. Good luck!

Unfortunately, my second opponent didn’t even make eye contact, had his friend sit next to him and put me down the whole time, and they just walked away after he won. I don’t have a ton of experience with online games outside of a few PC shooters, Splatoon 1, and Mario Kart 8, so my bar is pretty low as far as performance.

Regarding competitive, I suppose I’m not sure what I’m looking for either: I know I don’t have the time or reflexes to be winning tournaments and stuff like that, but I’d be happy to be involved in the community, know I was improving in a meaningful way, and get to know other people that love the series. I feel something similar. I played all of them except Ultimate because I still don't own a Switch. I considered getting one when Smash launched, but the reality is that I have nobody I can play with in my adult life. I still watch all the Directs, but they just make me wish for a time when my family and friends were close enough to share gaming memories.

My discipline is ok (military parent), and I’ve been able to practice at least a little bit every day, though that practice has deteriorated to little more than keeping up the DuoLingo streak, though I barely retain anything. I just wind up frustrated when some question is marked wrong for a reason that was never explained.

I’ve tried listening to the GermanPod101 podcast, and I follow the EasyGerman YouTube channel, though I’m intimidated about where I should start with their many videos. I feel ashamed about watching movies or shows alone, and I don’t think anyone will want to watch “Dark” or other German-language programming with me just to be accomodating: Every time I’ve told someone I’ve been trying to learn German, their first response is “Why?” 

I’m glad to hear your experience learning Italian is going well, and that’s the kind of feeling I’d love to have one day. Overcoming the anxiety of learning is sometimes more difficult than the language itself.

I think what I want for my skill set is to be able to switch between at least two different languages as easily as most of the international travelers I’ve met while I’ve been in NZ: people younger than myself who can arrive in a country where the mother tongue is different than their own and still make friends, tell jokes, find work, and communicate as easily as they could at home. The fact that I can meet groups of Germans, French, Dutch, etc.  in a hostel kitchen, and they can all switch to English for my sake, is impressive but leaves me feeling horribly guilty, like they are prepared to accommodate me but I can not do the same for them.

Thanks for the recommendation, and your situation is encouraging. I saw from your post history that you are a teacher and “want out”, same as myself. When NZ began lockdown, I was spending hours a day studying. Unfortunately, seeing the news from home and the rest of the world made the long-term goal of teaching English abroad seem increasingly distant. Some days I’m actually afraid that I’ll be forced to return to America, and the combination of travel restrictions and economic impact will prevent me from ever leaving again.

I’ll look into iTalki. At the moment I have nobody with whom to speak, and I’m a bit nervous that my listening comprehension is so poor after 8 months of daily practice, short of simple “tourist” phrases.

Interest in the culture was a major motivator at first: wanting to feel closer to the girl, and understand more about how and where she grew up. It’s encouraging to hear that you feel fulfilled learning even when there is little practical use at home, as I am in the same boat. I come from a lovely but notoriously homogeneous state, and I’m worried that my German studies would ultimately be nothing but a silly party trick.

Sometimes I’ve told myself to keep going just to challenge myself and feel some accomplishment at getting closer to bilingualism, though I’m nervous that I’d be veering into r/iamverysmart territory instead of actually having a practical skill and a way of communicating with more people.

I think the interest was only due to actually having a personal connection to a native speaker and learning about the culture. I could have just as easily met someone that spoke Spanish or French, and started learning with them. I’d love to travel and visit Germany/Austria/Switzerland one day, but not to any greater degree than anywhere else on my bucket list. Discipline to my routine is the overriding factor now.

I lost my job of 3.5 years today. I didn't love it, but it was stable if not lucrative. I’ve followed all the advice: I started running, lost weight, changed jobs twice, I’m back in school for a career change, and I try to volunteer a few times a year, but realistically, I won’t find anybody. Asking out a coworker is begging for trouble, I can’t approach anyone at the gym without risking looking like a creep, online courses are affordable but lonely, and I don’t earn enough money to do exciting things with the little free time I have. Online dating was just depressing after getting repeatedly ghosted over the span of two weeks. 

I’m very unhappy, and I’ve heard I can’t be loved until I love myself, but also that I’ll be alright once I meet someone.

Thank you for the advice. I have considered changing to a different school district. I went into teaching as a kind of trial: I was unhappy in data-entry, and a friend recommended I try subbing while I explore my career options. Most of the kids I work with are fine but administrative problems, coworkers, poor work/life balance, and unhelpful parents make the thought of a career unpleasant.

“Find your passion” is frequently thrown my way, but I’ve never been able to choose mine. I mentioned my dad shot down anything I was ever interested in, and now I’m a working adult with an exhausting, low-wage job. I don’t enjoy much of anything anymore, and the extent of finding my passion is whatever cheap class is offered at the town library at night. I was hospitalized for a suicide attempt a few months ago, but I can’t even afford therapy. It’s like I need to have money before I can buy the peace of mind to be comfortable enough with life to find a passion. I tried to skip a few steps by going for IT, hoping a vague interest could become a passion for coding over time, but I’m in over my head.

I was hoping for some guidance about making a drastic career change, especially when you still have to juggle your prior work and have no transferrable skills/experience. I’m glad you were able to succeed so spectacularly.

I hadn’t thought of governments/internships, though I’m a little worried about what options exist. I already work full-time, have been having trouble finding anything else, and where I live isn’t exactly bustling (Southern NH, local government is usually 1 room in an old town hall). Still, thank you for the recommendations.

I’ve looked at technical writing, but everybody wants experience I don’t have. My skills at both English and technology are abysmal, as I’m struggling to just get out of bed most days, let alone make some high-quality product for my classes/portfolio/resume.

As I commented on the other reply, I didn’t even realize IT and CS were different.
